newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing halts building in corruption crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Beijing halts building in corruption crackdown.

text.p: China's capital has ordered a three-year halt to construction of new office buildings by Beijing municipal and Communist party organisations in a drive to stamp out corruption, the China Daily said on Wednesday.

China's crackdown on corruption exposed 5,431 government or party officials involved in such crimes as embezzlement, bribery or misappropriation of public funds in the first five months of this year, the newspaper said.

In Beijing, the anti-corruption campaign has prompted authorities to declare a ban on construction of new office buildings by party and municipal organisations to combat waste and luxurious living by officials, it said.
In addition, the city's Communist Party Disciplinary Inspection Committee has cut back 18 new office projects, it said.
These reductions and the ban would help to save the city some 500 million yuan ($60.2 million), the committee said.
In addition, middle-ranking and senior officials whose telephones have been installed with public funds should cancel their international direct dialing function by the end of this month, it said.
Lower-ranking officials were ordered to pay their own telephone bills, after a monthly subsidy of 80 yuan ($9.60), it said.
China's anti-corruption drive moved into higher gear in Beijing in 1995 after Vice Mayor Wang Baosen committed suicide on a suburban hillside after coming under investigation for corruption.
The scandal led to the downfall of the city's Communist Party chief, Chen Xitong, who became the first member of the powerful Politburo to be purged for graft since the 1949 communist takeover.
However, corruption remained a problem and offenders should be severely punished, the newspaper said, quoting China's top prosecutors at a conference in Beijing.
The 5,431 people involved in corruption in the first five months were from party and government, from judicial organs and from economic management departments, the conference heard.
Many Chinese cite corruption among officials as their chief grievance, placing the issue even higher than inflation in their list of woes.
Communist Party chief and state president Jiang Zemin has warned that corruption is a virus that is so serious it could topple the ruling party if unchecked.
